## Abstract

<title>Abstract</title> Water scarcity and supply insecurity are the primary barriers to economic growth in arid and semi-arid regions. Inter-basin water transfer projects are high-cost solutions that could create socio-environmental side effects. This study presents a novel approach to optimally design such projects from an investor's perspective. We employed an energy input-output analysis-based linear programming (LP) model to determine the water demands of various economic sectors within an optimal development scenario. The results from this LP model, combined with a survey on the sectors' willingness to pay, are then integrated into a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) model formulated to optimally design the long-distance Khersan Dam-to-Kerman Province water conveyance project. The project is a 650-kilometer long water transfer line with a maximum pumping height of 800 meters whose cost is sensitive to its capacity to be optimized.

## Abstract

Streamflow uncertainty is one of the main challenges in managing reservoir systems. To accurately characterize the streamflow uncertainty in a reservoir operation model, numerous streamflow scenarios should be considered, but this results in a huge computational burden for multi-objective optimization. Here, we propose a methodology for deriving the operating rules for an inter-basin water transfer project (IBWT). The methodology adopts a scenario-reduction strategy to balance accuracy against the computational burden. The proposed method first reduces a large number of streamflow scenarios to several typical scenarios and the corresponding occurrence probabilities using a simultaneous backward reduction method. A multi-objective optimal operation model is then formulated to optimize the expected values of performance indices of the IBWT system under the typical scenarios. Finally, a simulation-based optimization framework is adopted to derive the multi-objective operating rules. To test the method, the Han to Wei IBWT project in northwest China is considered as a case study. The results show that the proposed methodology produces effective reservoir operating rules with a relatively low computational burden. After the initial 1,000 streamflow scenarios have been reduced to 20, the model solution time decreases significantly, from 49.17 h to 1.05 h, while the changes in mean value (0.47%) and standard deviation (0.93%) of these scenarios are less than 1%. Compared with an operation scheme that uses only historical streamflow data, the operation performance is further improved in terms of energy production, energy consumption, and water shortage index when the streamflow uncertainty is considered.

L34:   * cite19†Metrics details L35: ## Abstract
L36: Water scarcity and supply insecurity are the primary barriers to economic growth in arid and semi-arid regions. Inter-basin water transfer projects are high-cost solutions that could create socio-environmental side effects. This study presents a novel approach to optimally design such projects from an investor’s perspective. We employed an energy input–output analysis-based linear programming (LP) model to determine the water demands of various economic sectors within an optimal development scenario.
L37: The results from this LP model, combined with a survey on the sectors’ willingness to pay, are then integrated into a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) model formulated to optimally design the long-distance Khersan Dam-to-Kerman Province water conveyance project. The project is a 650-km long water transfer line with a cumulative pumping height of around 1500 m whose cost is sensitive to its capacity to be optimized.
L38: The model optimizes the project’s capacity based on the level of investment economically justified by the sectors demanding a sustainable water supply. Our findings indicate that approximately 85 percent of the increase in the water demand of Kerman’s economic activities (except agriculture, water provision, and service sectors) over the project’s lifetime could be met using only 5.2% of its total capacity.
L39: Furthermore, the financial participation of these economic activities could enhance the project’s net benefit by up to 6.3%.

L58: ## Introduction
L59: The uneven spatial and temporal distribution of Earth’s freshwater resources presents a fundamental challenge for water resources management. According to the United Nations, approximately 343 million people worldwide (5.8 percent of the global population) living in arid and semi-arid regions face water supply insecurity due to climate change and global warming^{cite26†1 }.
L60: Water resources management under drought conditions necessitates a transition from standard operating procedures to adaptive strategies that balance anthropogenic demand with ecological preservation.
L61: Policies to improve water security generally fall into two categories: a) supply-side policies, such as dam construction to address temporal unevenness and water transfer projects to address spatial unevenness, and b) demand-side policies, such as water markets, economic incentives (e.g., subsidies, taxes, and tariffs), and consumer education. The literature consistently prioritizes demand management over supply augmentation^{cite27†2 ,cite28†3 ,cite29†4 ,cite30†5 }.
L62: Nevertheless, supply-side solutions can become inevitable in cases of severe water scarcity.
L63: Inter-basin water transfer is a supply-side augmentation option designed to alleviate the uneven spatial distribution of water resources^{cite31†6 ,cite32†7 }. Globally prominent examples of such infrastructural megaprojects include China’s South-to-North Water Diversion^{cite33†8 }, the California State Water Project in the United States^{cite34†9 }, and the transboundary Lesotho Highlands Water Project in Southern Africa^{cite35†10 }.
L64: In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to integrated water transport and abstraction management strategies aimed at safeguarding critical water reservoirs that provide potable water and essential ecological services. In some cases where the water crisis is less severe, solutions such as allocation management can provide adaptation to water scarcity conditions.
L65: E.g, Lake Mead utilizes a tiered system where water delivery reductions are triggered by specific elevation thresholds, to manage systemic shortages in the Colorado River Basin^{cite36†11 ,cite37†12 }. Conversely, sever water shortage crises might require a combination of abstraction controls and large-scale water conveyance projects (WCPs).
L66: A prominent example is Lake Urmia, which lost over 80% of its surface area due to severe droughts and unsustainable anthropogenic withdrawals, resulting in hazardous salt storms. To combat this ecological disaster, the Zab River water transfer project was implemented. This megaproject systematically diverts approximately 600 million cubic meters of water annually to guarantee environmental flows, and stabilize the lake’s water levels^{cite38†13 }.
L67: The high costs and significant socio-environmental consequences of WCPs typically relegate these initiatives to one of the last resorts in water resource management hierarchies. Some scholars further contend that the legitimacy of such projects lies primarily in their capacity to supply drinking water, while other uses are viewed as less justifiable^{cite39†14 }. The case of Kerman Province in Iran is one such example. Kerman is the largest province in Iran, with a total area of 183,285 sq.
L68: km, and is located in an arid region with a mean annual precipitation of 134 mm^{cite40†15 }. Groundwater resources provide 87 percent of the potable water and 95 percent of the total water supply in Kerman^{cite41†16 }. However, the province’s main aquifers have experienced drastic declines due to over-exploitation, with an average water level drop of more than 0.5 m per year over the past two decades.
L69: Consequently, water supply security for all purposes, especially for drinking water which requires higher quality and reliability, has been seriously endangered^{cite42†2 }.
L70: The water crisis in Kerman has prompted government action, leading to plans for the construction of a costly WCP known as the Khersan Dam Conveyance Line (KDCL). The KDCL is designed to transfer water from the Karun Basin to Kerman over a distance of 640 km. Although there is a consensus that the KDCL is a practical solution to Kerman’s water shortage, stakeholders have yet to agree on the volume of water to be transferred.
L71: A key dispute revolves around the necessity of supplying water for productive sectors in addition to meeting drinking and sanitation needs. Policy-makers are seeking to share the cost of KDCL with the productive sectors, but the financing of the KDCL present a dilemma. On one hand, the project involves high fixed costs, which implies a declining unit cost of water as the project’s scale increases.
L72: On the other hand, the enormous expense of water supply via the KDCL could render the expansion of water-intensive industries either practically infeasible or economically unjustified. Therefore, determining the optimal scale of the project and the corresponding volume of water to be transferred remains a critical question.
L73: Several studies have examined inter-basin WCPs from technical^{cite33†8 }, social^{cite43†17 }, environmental^{cite44†18 }, legal^{cite45†19 }, and economic^{cite46†20 } perspectives. Han, et al.^{cite33†8 } developed a Copula-Bayesian coupling framework to examine how often and under what circumstances wet versus dry conditions in the source basin encounter matching or mismatching hydrological states in the receiving basin.
L74: Wei, et al.^{cite43†17 } applied game theory to simulate and resolve water allocation and nitrogen reduction conflicts in the Middle Route of China’s South-to-North water transfer project. Ding, et al.^{cite44†18 } quantified the impact of the Yangtze-to-Huaibe Water Diversion Project’s construction on land use and the supply–demand balance of Ecosystem Services in the Anhui section.
L75: Wang and Li^{cite45†19 } Examined how China’s institutions have adapted (or failed to adapt) to manage the middle route of the South-to-North Transfer, with emphasis on legal frameworks, governance, institutional fragmentation, and policy mandates. Cao, et al.^{cite46†20 } developed a multi-scenario optimization model to improve the operation of inter-basin water transfer systems by explicitly balancing transfer costs and supply reliability.
L76: Among the studies evaluating WCPs from an economic perspective, many emploied simulation–optimization approaches to perform cost–benefit analyses (CBA)^{cite30†5 ,cite47†21 ,cite48†22 ,cite49†23 ,cite50†24 }. Draper, et al.^{cite51†25 } proposed an economic–engineering optimization framework for the California water supply system, demonstrating the practicality of optimization models with economic objectives for large-scale water resources management.
L77: To achieve a more comprehensive CBA, researchers have attempted to quantify the costs of environmental and social impacts of WCPs by incorporating them into the analysis as additional economic variables^{cite31†6 ,cite46†20 ,cite50†24 }. However, the economic benefits of WCPs are still often restricted to revenues from water sales to specific, predefined users—typically farmers^{cite31†6 ,cite52†23 ,cite50†24 ,cite53†26 }.
L78: E.g, Nasiri-Gheidari, et al.^{cite50†24 } developed a multi-objective optimization model to identify an optimal water transfer pattern that minimizes environmental pollution while maximizing economic benefits for the initial plan of the KDCL project; yet their analysis assumes agriculture as the sole beneficiary of the transferred water.
L79: While a number of studies have applied economic models—such as computable general equilibrium (CGE) and energy input–output analysis (EIOA) frameworks—to assess the economic impacts of WCPs on donor and recipient regions^{cite54†21 ,cite55†22 ,cite56†27 ,cite57†28 ,cite58†29 }, they rarely address the optimal hydraulic design of the conveyance system^{cite59†30 ,cite60†31 }.
L80: simultaneous consideration of both aspects is essential for developing an optimal WCP plan, as the unit cost of water transfer depends directly on the project’s scale and capacity, whereas the transfer volume should be determined by demand-side factors, including customers’ willingness to pay (WTP)^{cite61†32 }. Accordingly, outputs from the economic model should inform a conveyance-line optimization model to determine the project’s optimal capacity.
L81: This study employs an EIOA model to incorporate the economic structure of the receiving region of the WCP and resource consumption scenarios^{cite62†33 } into the optimization of the KDCL project design. Using an EIOA-based linear programming (LP) model, water demand for different economic sectors is determined under the optimal development scenario, i.e., maximizing economic growth in Kerman province.
L82: The EIOA model also estimates the water intensity of each economic sector, which is combined with survey data from production units to calculate their willingness to pay (WTP) for water. These water demand and WTP values are used to construct a discrete benefit function for different volumes of transferred water.
L83: Recognizing that the volume of water transfer influences both the conveyance line design and the unit cost of water provision, this study considered mutual effect of them to provide a more comprehensive solution. Therefore, the resulting benefit function is incorporated into a MINLP model to determine the cost of water provision and identify the optimal design of the WCP.
L84: The paper is structured as follows. The following section of Methods and Materials introduces the case study, and shows how data required for developing the EIOA model are collected and used. It then explains how the EIOA and cost estimation models are consolidated within an optimization problem framework; then it presents the formulation of the optimization problem developed based on the cost estimation equations and the outcome of the EIOA model.
L85: The results and discussion section provides the outputs of the optimization problem, including the optimal design of the project and optimal water transfer plan. Finally, the conclusion section summarizes all discussions and provides suggestions for future studies.
L86: ## Methods and materials
L87: ### Case study
L88: With a total area of 183.2 km^{2}, Kerman Province is the largest province of Iran. Similar to other provinces located in the eastern strip of the country, it suffers from severe water shortages. According to the 2016 population census, Kerman’s population is 3.2 million and contributes 3.7% to Iran’s GDP (excluding oil), with the industry, agriculture, and mining sectors producing 1.76, 1.9, and 0.7 billion USD, respectively^{cite63†34 }.
L89: Water scarcity is one of the main barriers to economic development in Kerman^{cite64†35 }. Kerman’s water supply relies on local surface and groundwater resources, providing 10.5% and 89.5% of the total water supply, respectively, i.e., 5598 MCM/year^{cite41†16 }. The groundwater level in Kerman has declined by approximately 0.5 m per year over the past two decades. Similarly, surface runoff has decreased by more than 35% compared to its long-term average (IWPC, 2020).
L90: In addition, groundwater quality has been poor and continues to deteriorate; the concentration of heavy metals—particularly arsenic—in some aquifer sections is ten times higher than the drinking water standard (INWW Eng. Co., 2020). These conditions indicate that Kerman’s local water resources will be insufficient to meet even the drinking water demand, estimated to increase by 1.6% annually and reach 561 MCM by 2045, neither quantitatively nor qualitatively.
L91: Agricultural activities consume about 92% of the total water supply, and agricultural water use has remained almost constant over the past decade. Beyond water quality concerns, meeting drinking water demand by reducing agricultural withdrawals is highly challenging, largely due to the difficulty of persuading local farmers. Consequently, the KDCL project has become a government priority in the region.
L92: As depicted in the spatial layout of the KDCL project (Fig. cite65†1 ), the 650-km conveyance line traverses substantial topographical obstacles, extending from the Karun Basin through the Zagros Mountain Range to Kerman (Fig. cite66†4 ). Notwithstanding an elevation differential of approximately 100 m between the origin and destination sites, a cumulative pumping head of roughly 1,500 m is required to facilitate water transfer along the conveyance path.
L93: This configuration necessitates a hydraulic design incorporating multiple high-head pumping stations and pressure-reducing valves (PRVs). Furthermore, the deployment of pipelines with higher pressure classes is imperative.
L94: While the primary purpose of the KDCL is to supply drinking water, it could secure water supply for the economic activities, except agriculture and services, with an annual water need of only around 55 MCM and a high share of gross domestic production (GDP) (63 percent of Kerman’s GDP)^{cite63†34 }. Thus, the project has the potential to act as a driver of regional economic development. Moreover, supplying water to economic activities could partially finance this high-cost project.

L102: ### Modeling approach
L103: The methodology adopted in this study involves quantifying the costs and benefits of water supply to different economic sectors and then solving a combinatorial nonlinear optimization model to determine both the optimal volume of water transfer and the project’s design variables, including pipeline dimensions and length, the capacity and location of pumping stations, the placement of pressure reduction valves (PRVs), pipe’s working pressure and flow velocity.
L104: The model’s objective function maximizes the net benefit of the project, defined as the difference between the water price in the donor and receiving regions minus the cost of water provision. While the unit cost of water provision generally decreases with project scale, the WTP of water users declines as the transfer volume increases^{cite69†36 }. Clearly, the optimal solution is achieved when the marginal cost of water provision equals the marginal WTP of consumers.
L105: Figure cite70†2 illustrates the procedure used to derive the optimal plan for the KDCL project. The proposed model comprises two separate modules, i.e., cost and benefit estimation modules, which are incorporated simultaneously into the optimization model. In the cost estimation module, several variables and parameters, including project scale and electricity price, influence the design of the conveyance line and, consequently, the unit cost of water provision.
L106: These variables and parameters are functionally dependent and interact through governing flow equations and design criteria. To capture these relationships, a simulation model was developed based on the KDCL project’s initial plan proposed by Iran Water and Power Resources Development Co. (IWPC), as the KDCL project client. Using defined technical standards, construction price lists, and design equations, simulation model estimate the cost of water provision at different transfer volumes.

L114: The benefit estimation module quantifies the economic gains from water sales by incorporating both the economic sectors’ WTP for water and their projected water demand. L115: An EIOA-based linear programming model (Eqs. cite73†7 to cite74†11 ) was employed to identify the optimal development pattern under water scarcity, determining the expansion trajectory of the economic sectors during the project operation period. The WTP of the sectors was estimated using a function fitted to data from selected production units, linking their water use intensity with WTP.
L116: These data were obtained from contract records provided by the Iran National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company, where the prices agreed upon in water sales contracts served as the basis for calculating WTP. The outcomes of these estimations were used to derive the relationship between water supply and the corresponding benefit was derived and incorporated as a discrete function into the optimization model presented in the following section.
L117: It is important to note that the proposed methodology is developed based on the following key assumptions. First, the significant decline in groundwater levels is assumed to constrain further abstraction from local sources, implying that any additional water demand must be satisfied through the KDCL project. Second, a portion of the drinking water supply is anticipated to be provided via seawater desalination.
L118: ### Optimization model
L119: The optimization model proposed in this study involves a simple CBA (Eqs. cite75†1 to cite76†4 ) to assess the cost-effectiveness of supplying water to Kerman’s economic activities. The term \({Benefit}_{Total}\) in the model is calculated using the benefit estimation module (Eqs. cite77†5 to cite78†8 ), which incorperate the demands estimated by the EIOA-based LP model and water sale tariffs determined according to WTP of the economic sectors to estimate revenues for different water transfer volumes.
L120: Water transfer volume affects the project costs, including the implementation \((Cos{t}^{Imp})\) and operation \((Cos{t}_{PV}^{Opr})\) costs, calculated via the cost estimation module (Eqs. cite79†16 to cite80†35 ). By simultaneously solving the cost and benefit equations, the model determines the optimal water transfer volume and other design variables. The presence of discrete variables and non-linear relationships in this model converts it to a MINLP, an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem.

L141: Equations cite83†6 to cite78†8 form the benefit estimation module of the optimization model developed to maximize the net benefit of the KDCL project. As outlined earlier, project benefits include revenues from water sales to economic sectors, priced according to their marginal willingness to pay (WTP), and revenues from potable water supplied to households at the regulated tariff (Eq. cite77†5 ).

L33: همان طور که اشاره کردید یکی از مشکلات محیط زیست و مناطق ما پدیده «تغییر اقلیم» است که علاوه بر کاهش بسترهای رشد آن، باید برای تاب آوری و سازگاری با آن برنامه داشت. آیا سازمان در این باره برنامه ای تدوین کرده است؟
L34: بر اساس قانون برنامه هفتم، شش آیین نامه را امسال در دولت مصوب کردیم که یکی از آنها درباره «برنامه مدیریت تغییر اقلیم» بود. جلسات متعددی داشتیم با دستگاه های مختلف و توانستیم برنامه مدیریت تغییر اقلیم را تصویب کنیم. از موضوعاتی که در ارتباط با این آیین نامه شاخص هستند، این است که علاوه بر کاهش انتشار گازهای گلخانه ای، به موضوع «سازگاری با تغییر اقلیم» که بسیار مهم است نیز توجه شود.
L35: متاسفانه کشور ما به دلیل موقعیت جغرافیایی، در زمره کشورهایی است که تاثیرپذیری بالایی را از پیامدهای تغییر اقلیم تجربه کرده اند که از مهم ترین آنها می توان به کاهش 40 درصدی میزان بارش ها در کشور و افزایش مصرف انرژی بر اثر افزایش دما اشاره کرد. برای مقابله با پدیده تغییر اقلیم، تدوین یک راهبرد و برنامه جامع ملی، یک ضرورت اجتناب ناپذیر است. این راهبرد به کشور اجازه می دهد به جای واکنش انفعالی، به پیامدهای تغییر اقلیم به صورت فعالانه و برنامه ریزی شده عمل کند.
L36: یعنی ما علاوه بر اینکه کشوری در زمره کشورهایی با میزان بالای گازهای گلخانه ای هستیم و باید در زمینه کاهش انتشار کار کنیم، باید به واسطه متاثر بودن از پدیده تغییر اقلیم، روی برنامه تاب آوری و سازگاری نیز کار کنیم. الگوی کشت متناسب و سازگار با اقلیم داشته باشیم یا در مباحث مدیریت مصرف انرژی و آب به محدودیت های پیش رو توجه کنیم. از ظرفیت های دیگر برنامه مدیریت تغییر اقلیم، پیش بینی سازوکار «بازار داوطلبانه ملی کربن» است.
L37: اقدامات مالیات کربن توسط اتحادیه اروپا و دیگر کشورهای جهان، بیانگر تغییر در رویکرد این کشورها بر واردات محصولات پرکربن به داخل مرزهای خود است که تحت عنوان تعرفه های زیست محیطی، توان رقابتی و حاشیه سود محصولات صادراتی کشور را تحت تاثیر قرار خواهد داد و منجر به کاهش ارزآوری به کشور می شود. بنابراین صنایع صادراتی انرژی بر در کشور، در صورت عدم جبران میزان انتشار گازهای گلخانه ای خارج از حد استاندارد از طریق خرید گواهی کربن، آسیب خواهند دید.
L38: یکی از اقدامات مقابله ای موثر داخلی برای کاهش انتشار، بازار کربن و راه اندازی نظام MRV ملی مطابق با استانداردهای بین المللی است که با جذب سرمایه گذاری بخش خصوصی، نه تنها انگیزه های اقتصادی برای کاهش انتشار و کاهش مصرف انرژی را فراهم می کند، بلکه باعث نوآوری در فناوری و حفظ محیط زیست از جمله کاهش آلاینده های محلی و کاهش مصرف انرژی می شود.
L39: یکی از دغدغه های متخصصان و کنشگران حوزه محیط زیست و منابع طبیعی، ارزش گذاری منابع محیط زیستی و خدمات اکوسیستمی است که عمدتا نه به آنها توجه می شود و نه اجرایی. در خبرها آمد که آیین نامه آن در سالی که گذشت به تصویب دولت رسید. آیا می توان به اجرای این آیین نامه امیدوار بود؟
L40: بله، همین طور است. یکی دیگر از آیین نامه هایی که امسال به تصویب دولت رسیده، «ارزش گذاری خدمات اکوسیستمی» بوده که از قانون برنامه چهارم مطرح بوده ولی تاکنون مصوبه دولت نداشته است. شکل گیری این باور که خدمات به ظاهر رایگان اکوسیستم ها در حقیقت دارایی های گرانبهایی اند که تخریب یا آلودگی ناشی از فعالیت های انسانی می تواند با کاهش آنها، سلامت، رفاه و پایداری جامعه را تهدید کند؛ نبود سازوکار مشخص برای محاسبه و جبران این خسارات، یکی از مهم ترین خلاهای موجود در زمینه حفاظت از محیط زیست بود.
L41: یقینا اجرای دقیق و شفاف این آیین نامه می تواند معادله ای جدید میان توسعه و حفاظت ایجاد کند. معادله ای که در آن محیط زیست، دیگر بازنده همیشگی پروژه های توسعه ای نباشد. امیدواریم با توجه به مصوبه دولت، بتوانیم خدمات اکوسیستمی را به لحاظ اقتصادی، ارزش گذاری کنیم تا بتوانیم در برابر درخواست های واگذاری و توسعه، با زبان اقتصاد، اهمیت این موضوع را برای تصمیم گیران تفهیم کنیم که مثلا ارزش این اکوسیستم آنقدر هست و قابل جایگزینی نیست.
L42: همچنین بر اساس این آیین نامه دستگاه های اجرایی، شرکت ها، سرمایه گذاران و همه عاملان ایجاد هزینه های محیط زیستی موظف می شوند تا در فرآیند اجرای طرح ها، هزینه های محیط زیستی را برآورد کنند و با اجتناب از وارد کردن هزینه در وهله اول، هزینه های جبران آثار و پیامدهای غیرقابل اجتناب را محاسبه و تامین کنند.
L43: هوای ناسالم به ویژه در کلانشهرها همچنان در اغلب ماه های سال در حال هجوم به سلامت شهروندان و حتی مناطق طبیعی است. در این باره سازمان چه برنامه ای دارد؟
L44: «کارگروه ملی کاهش آلودگی هوا» که مدتی غیرفعال بود؛ از ابتدای دولت با حضور مستمر معاون اجرایی رییس جمهور که رییس کارگروه است و سایر دستگاه های اجرایی، در بالاترین سطح تشکیل شد. یکی از مصوبات این کارگروه «اسقاط خودروهای فرسوده» بود. در «قانون هوای پاک» به عنوان یکی از مهم ترین اسناد بالادستی مدیریت آلودگی هوا، یکی از محورهای مهم که باید به آن توجه می شد، اسقاط ناوگان فرسوده است. در کشور 24 میلیون خودروی فرسوده وجود دارد؛ رقمی قابل توجه.
L45: ولی مجموع کاری که طی 8-7 سال اخیر بعد از تصویب قانون هوای پاک برای خودروهای فرسوده انجام شد، اسقاط 200 هزار خودرو بود؛ 24 میلیون خودرو فرسوده داریم. طی 7 سال بعد از تصویب قانون، 200 هزار خودرو اسقاط شده اند؛ در حالی که بر اساس همان قانون باید در هر سال 500 هزار خودرو اسقاط می شد. ما از سال گذشته این موضوع را پیگیری کردیم. در این یک سال و نیم 500 هزار خودرو اسقاط شده که در مقایسه با سال های قبل یک رکورد است، ولی کافی نیست.
L46: برای پیشبرد کار، ابزار تشویقی باید باشد و دیگر اینکه در ازای گواهی اسقاط واقعا خودروی فرسوده اسقاط شود و به چرخه حمل ونقل برنگردد.
L47: برای موتورسیکلت های فرسوده و آلاینده که تعدادشان در ناوگان حمل و نقل شهری کلانشهرها و نقش شان در آلودگی هوا رو به افزایش است هم برنامه ای دارید؟
L48: در ارتباط با موتورسیکلت های فرسوده هم برنامه هایی در دست اقدام است. پیش از این هیچ برنامه ای برای موتورسیکلت ها وجود نداشت؛ در حالی که همان طور که اشاره کردید بخش بزرگی از ناوگان حمل و نقل عمومی را موتورسیکلت ها تشکیل می دهند. در تهران، از شهرداری و استانداری خواستیم به عنوان یک فاز آزمایشی، 20 هزار موتورسیکلت های کار را در فاز اول با موتورسیکلت برقی جایگزین کنند. کار تا مراحلی جلو رفت، ولی به دلیل برخی موانع اجرایی، روند کار کند شده است؛ ولی ما پیگیر هستیم.
L49: البته می دانیم این تعداد خیلی کم است و این برنامه باید در فازبندی جلو برود. همچنین زیرساخت های توسعه خودروها و موتورسیکلت های برقی مانند ایستگاه شارژ و... هم باید تامین شود تا شهروندان تمایل به استفاده از آن داشته باشند.
L50: مشکل شرکت در کنوانسیون های بین المللی چه بود؟ اخباری درباره حذف حق رای سازمان محیط زیست ایران منتشر شد و اینکه ایران کاملا منزوی شده است.
L51: مشکلی در بحث های بین المللی حوزه محیط زیست وجود داشت که به بدهی های انباشته بین المللی ایران مربوط می شد و ما را از برخی ارتباطات در این زمینه محروم کرده بود. بدهی های انباشته ای که بالغ بر 10 سال حق عضویت ایران در کنوانسیون های مختلف پرداخت نشده و مانده بود.
L52: از آن طرف ارزش ریال پایین آمده و به نحوی شده بود که مثلا کنوانسیون راپمی ROPME که مربوط به محیط زیست منطقه خلیج فارس و دریای عمان است به ما اعلام کرده بودند که دیگر حق رای ندارید یا مثلا برای کنوانسیون رامسر که اولین کنوانسیون محیط زیستی جهان در حوزه تالاب ها بوده و به اسم شهر رامسر ما هست و مرکز منطقه ای داریم، یکی از کشورهای عربی پیگیر بود که این مرکز را به خاطر عدم عملکرد از کشور ما بگیرند.
L53: بر این اساس ما با یک چالش جدی روبه رو بودیم؛ از آن طرف کمبود منابع مالی و از طرف دیگر ضرورت حضور فعال در کنوانسیون های بین المللی محیط زیست بود. لذا بدهی ها را اولویت بندی کردیم؛ مثلا 4 میلیون دلار بدهی انباشته کنوانسیون راپمی بود. بخشی را پرداختیم تا بتوانیم حق رای داشته باشیم. برای حیثیت و اقتدار کشورمان هم درست نبود. کشوری که واقعا از نظر مساحت، جمعیت و منابع، بزرگ ترین و مهم ترین کشور در حوزه خلیج فارس است به خاطر عدم پرداخت بدهی نتواند حق رای داشته باشد.
L54: سال گذشته از طریق سازمان برنامه و بودجه پیگیری کردیم و 250 هزار یورو از بدهی های معوقه را پرداخت کردیم. الان باز پیگیر هستیم که مابقی را بتوانیم به صورت تدریجی با اولویت مواردی که پرداخت نشده، تادیه کنیم. برای کنوانسیون رامسر که پشتیبان 15 کشور منطقه است و سال ها دبیرخانه آن در کشور ما بوده، از زمانی که در سال 1349 کنوانسیون رامسر شکل گرفته است، خوشبختانه رایزنی کردیم و برای سه سال توانستیم فعالیت مرکز رامسر را تمدید کنیم.
L55: در حال حاضر هم پیگیر ارتقای عملکرد مرکز و فعالیت منطقه ای آن هستیم؛ ضمن اینکه در یک سال گذشته توانستیم سند ساختمان مرکز رامسر را اخذ کنیم.
L56: درباره تفویض اختیار استانداران، روایت های متفاوت و نقدهایی وجود دارد. آیا شامل مسائل محیط زیستی هم می شود؟ با توجه به اینکه استانداران در تمام دولت ها اغلب با مباحث جدید علمی در حوزه محیط زیست بیگانه هستند و این تفویض اختیار می تواند پیامدهای بی بازگشتی داشته باشد.
L57: درباره تفویض اختیار استانداران جلسات متعددی داشتیم و تاکید داشتیم که بسیاری از موضوعات محیط زیستی قابل تفویض نیست، چراکه جزو مباحث حاکمیتی است که باید متمرکز راجع به آن تصمیم گیری شود. در عین حال 33 وظیفه را که قابل واگذاری بود مانند استعلام های مجوز استقرار، تفویض اختیار کردیم. از جمله اقدامات شاخص در یک سال و نیم گذشته در حوزه محیط زیست، می توانم به پتروشیمی میانکاله اشاره کنم که مصوبه دولت را گرفتیم، چون مصوبه قبلی داشت برای استقرار پتروشیمی و ما مصوبه را لغو کردیم که پتروشیمی اینجا نباید مستقر بشود.
L58: علاوه بر آن، زمین باید برگردد که این موضوع را باید جهاد کشاورزی پیگیری کند به عنوان اراضی ملی. تله کابین گرگان که خود شما در جریان موضوع هستید دو، سه بار اعلام کرده بودیم و در نهایت از ما خواستند نظر صریح را بدهیم که در محل پیشنهادی با توجه به پیامدهای محیط زیستی اعلام مخالفت کردیم. در واقع ما با تله کابین مشکل نداریم، ولی جانمایی نباید دارای عوارض مخرب محیط زیستی باشد.
L59: اخباری به گوش می رسد درباره اینکه سند تالاب ها به نام سازمان محیط زیست نباشد؛ آیا درست است؟
L60: درباره تالاب ها، این اواخر مشکلاتی وجود داشت که البته مدیریت پیشین سازمان زحمت کشیده بودند برای اینکه سند تالاب ها به نمایندگی دولت به نام سازمان محیط زیست باشد. باز در این دوره پیگیری هایی انجام شد برای اینکه این اتفاق نیفتد؛ حتی بخشنامه ای هم ابلاغ شد. نهایتا ما پیگیری کردیم و دستور رییس سازمان ثبت اسناد و املاک کشور را گرفتیم. الان سند 16 تالاب به نمایندگی دولت به نام سازمان حفاظت محیط زیست صادر شده است. البته موضوع مهم تر درباره تالاب ها، بحث حقابه تالاب هاست!
L61: دقیقا این سوال بعدی من است؛ هر اقدامی برای نجات تالاب، بدون دریافت حقابه بی نتیجه است. چرا سازمان محیط زیست نمی تواند حقابه تالاب ها را که امری قانونی است از وزارت نیرو بگیرد؟
L62: در قوانین بالادستی و آیین نامه تالاب ها، بعد از آب شرب، اولویت دوم، آب طبیعت و حقابه محیط زیست است؛ ولی در واقعیت چه اتفاقی می افتد؟ بعد از آب شرب، ما آب صنعت را باید بدهیم؛ آب کشاورزی را بدهیم؛ به خاطر اینکه قسمت عمده آب کشور در این بخش استفاده می شود. شاید لازم باشد مثلا یک سال در تهران یا مناطق دیگر طرح نکاشت را اجرا کنیم تا آب بیاید جذب آبخوان و طبیعت شود و این فرونشست هایی که واقعا در بعضی مناطق بسیار نگران کننده است قدری تعدیل شود. به هر حال ما پیگیر هستیم ولی شرایط کشور را هم باید ببینیم.
L63: مشکلات در حوزه محیط زیست بسیار زیاد است و با شرایط اجتماعی و اقتصادی که کشور با آن روبه رو است، مدیریت این همه مساله بسیار دشوار و پیچیده است. از طرفی ما به خاطر ماهیت کارمان در خیلی از مباحث مطالبه گر هستیم؛ در بحث آب، حقابه و حتی در بحث سوخت. امسال در راستای شفافیت، گزارشی منتشر کردیم در پاییز درباره کیفیت سوخت و میزان پارامترهای آلاینده را در آن تشریح کردیم. مثلا سوخت بنزین، به چه میزان بنزن و ترکیبات آروماتیک دارد یا سوخت گازوییل چه مقدار محتوی گوگرد دارد. در جلسه دولت هم این گزارش را ارایه کردم.
L64: خوشبختانه پایش های بعدی ما و «سازمان ملی استاندارد» نشان داد که وضعیت در کلانشهرها تا حد زیادی بهبود یافته است. ما معتقدیم که باید در محورهای مختلف محیط زیست گزارش های تخصصی بدهیم و وضعیت را شفاف بگوییم. در بحث آب هم همین طور است. گاهی با توجه به شرایطی که در بحث آب داریم باید جسارت در تصمیم گیری داشته باشیم. فراموش نکنیم که در شرایط فقر، حفظ محیط زیست دشوارتر می شود. به عبارتی هر چه جامعه فقیرتر شود، دست درازی به منابع طبیعی افزایش پیدا می کند. این یک اصل محرز است.
L65: وقتی جامعه فقیرتر شود، شکار بیشتر می شود؛ قاچاق حیات وحش شدت می گیرد. تعارضات و دست اندازی ها افزایش می یابد. از آن طرف نگرانی های ما برای محیط بانان واقعا بیشتر می شود، چون محیط بانان ما باید با حجم تخلفاتی که رخ می دهد، مقابله کنند. به همین دلیل باید حفاظت را مشارکتی و از نیروهای بومی و محلی در حفاظت استفاده کنیم. این، یکی از رویکردهای سازمان است؛ مدلی که امروز در جهان مرسوم و موفق بوده است.
L66: در این راستا در «شورای عالی محیط زیست» در دی ماه سال جاری افزایش حفاظت گاه های مردمی را طرح و بررسی کردیم. تجربه خوبی هم در «پارک ملی گلستان» در موضوع حفاظت مشارکتی بوده که افزایش حفاظت گاه های مردمی را داشته باشیم. 7 حفاظت گاه مردمی در شورای عالی محیط زیست تصویب شد که هم به ما و هم به افزایش جمعیت حیات وحش کمک می کند.

L79: By the People’s Campaign to Save the Kind Zagros, supporter of cite34†Save the Tigris Campaign†www.savethetigris.org L80: Iranian environmentalists annually celebrate the International Day Against Water Transfer on 17 April, or 28 Favardin, according to the Persian calendar. Water transfers between watersheds are common practice in Iran. They have been regarded as one of the most effective ways to reduce water scarcity, as many Iranian politicians have advocated. Such water scarcity is caused by the differences in distribution of water resources, population growth, and damage caused by floods and droughts.
L81: The reality, however, is that the discussions around water transfer projects have been overly simplified despite their social, economic, political, technical, and environmental complexities. Such complications have been exacerbated due to lack of comprehensive and accurate impact assessments. Water transfer projects have often been implemented in a speedy manner.
L82: They are assessed only from an engineering perspective and lack accurate expert evaluation that would take into account the effects of regional basin management and the impacts on future generations. Opponents argue that water transfer projects have been securitized and are imposed on society and the environment despite widespread opposition.
L83: Each inter-basin water transfer plan contains at least two separate basins: the basin of destination — where the water is to be transferred to, and the source basin — upstream from where the water is to be transferred. Inter-basin water transfer is an operation that transfers water from one watershed to another in order to supply water for agriculture, control flooding, generate electricity, and supply water for industrial and domestic use.
L84: Usually, the upstream watersheds consist of mountainous and hilly lands and contain forests, rangeland, or cultivated land. The destination shed consists of a lower slope containing mostly agricultural and urban infrastructure as well as water storage tanks and irrigation canals.
L85: Currently in the inter-basin water transfer programs implemented within Iran, only the destination basin benefits from the transfer, while the populations of upstream water basins often do not benefit despite being in need of economic development. The livelihood of upstream populations mostly consists of livestock and agriculture. Water transfer projects threaten these livelihoods in addition to the damage they cause to social and cultural ties between affected communities.
L86: In contrast, the destination basin benefits from the water stored in dam reservoirs for consumption, industry, and agriculture. Their populations are usually rural and urban middle class who have access to amenities.
L87: Opponents claim that water transfer projects in Iran are based on false assumptions and exaggerated water needs of the destination basin, arguing that levels of water supplies of the source basins are questionable, and the effects of climate change are not properly considered. Other options, such as demand management, have not sufficiently been explored and, most importantly, the potential for conflicts between source and destination basins have not been assessed.
L88: Environmental impact assessments in the source and destination basins are rarely conducted and adverse social consequences have not been studied well. Economically, the justifications for water projects are questionable, and the planning and decision-making processes lack transparency and public participation.
L89: Populations around source basins have protested against water transfer projects and their future negative consequences but have not received sufficient media or public attention. On 17 April 2014, one of the largest environmental demonstrations in recent Iranian history took place. The rally was attended by 30,000 people from Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari Province. Since then, the date has been commemorated as the International Day Against Water Transfer.
L90: It has been supported by environmental organizations across Iran, from those opposing water transfers in the Lesser Zab basin, from the Caspian Sea to the Central plateau, and from Jiroft to Kerman. The International Day Against Water Transfer is marked as an opportunity to draw attention to the negative impacts of water transfer projects in Iran and a call for solidarity from international civil society in the struggle against dam, water transfer, and other environmentally destructive projects.

However, despite awareness raising, we still witness ignorance of about the vital importance of water resources through destructive and costly dam construction and inter-basin water transfers in Iran.
L103: Gigantic water transfer projects are underway in Iran such as Khersan, Sabzkooh, Behesht-Abad, Koohrang 3 Dam, Vanak-Rafsanjan and Gulab on the Karun River, Alborz to Tehran on the Karaj River, Jiroft to Kerman on the Halil River, and other dam projects such as Lori, Bakhtiari, Lesser Zab, and dozens of other similar projects are under construction.
L104: In addition, the Ministry of Energy plans to implement an alarming project to transfer water from the Caspian Sea to Semnan and expensive and energy-intensive projects to transfer water from the southern seas to areas around the country. The current policies and actions of the Ministry demonstrate that the health of rivers and other bodies of water is being given little priority.
L105: The structural mindset that dominates the Ministry continues to degrade the health of bodies of water in the country and negatively affect those who depend on them.
L106: On the occasion of International Day of Action Against Water Transfer (17 April 2021 / 28 Farvardin 1400), we, as environmental activists, in convergence with people who love the nature of this province, will continue to defend the vitality of its largest river, Karun, and engage in the global proceedings protecting rivers and the environment to stop environmental destruction under the deceptive practice of “improving the water supply”.

L108: As authors of this statement:
L109:   * We believe that dam construction and inter-basin water transfer is among the largest threats to the life of rivers and their inhabitants, and we consider it our duty to strive for the protection of waterways, rectifying environmental water rights, and observe the natural rights of people living around rivers, lakes, and estuaries.
L110:   * We believe that continuing water transfer programs will have dangerous social, economic, and environmental consequences and result in internal displacement and emigration.
L111:   * We ask the honourable Judiciary to seriously address corruption in water transfer and dam construction projects, to criminalize environmental damage, take the necessary measures to prosecute criminals in this area, and accelerate environmental cases opened in the courts.
L112:   * We request that necessary mechanisms be established, including special environmental courts, and that the Constitutional Court address violations of national law regarding water projects.
L113:   * We call for the legistlation of a “Comprehensive Water Law” which takes into account the Supreme Leader’s(I) document on general environmental policies, considers the socio-environmental impacts of water projects, and includes the meaningful participation of civil society and local stakeholders.
L114:   * We ask the honourable Islamic Consultative Assembly(II) to immediately investigate dam construction and water transfer projects that have recently been added to its agenda.
L115:   * We call for the dissolution of the Supreme Council of Water(III) and reconstituting the mechanism as a participatory and democratic “Water Parliament”.
L116:   * We call for serious protection of the country’s pastures and forests, non-structural management on aquifers and watersheds, and the prevention of mining and other activities that may lead to irreparable damage to the environment.
L117:   * We call for major reforms in irrigation methods, the cessation of quantitative development of agricultural lands, and for changes in water consumption patterns in all sectors to reduce consumption and adapt to new climatic conditions.

This report "Transformation Strategies in Agriculture" is one outcome of the project “Integrated Water Resources Management Zayandeh Rud (IWRM)” (3/2016-12/2018), funded by BMBF. 
It is the result of a strongly interactive process with local stakeholders designed and moderated in a cooperation between the German and Iranian project partners. The information gained in through the participatory process was synthesized into ten transformation strategies that are grouped into four focus areas (Capacity Development, Agricultural Management, Water Distribution, and Land Management and Soil Fertility). The participatory process and the resulting strategies with measures for their implementation are detailed in this report.

Important for the success of the agricultural transformation is the willingness of governments, farmers, donors, companies and civil society organizations to assume responsibilities, take risks and change behaviors at the level of individuals, organizations and society to pursue an accepted solution within the basin. Key to all the proposed transformation strategies in the report are activities to continue the development of a common knowledge base and set of tools, so that integrated resource management plans can be put forward and continually evaluated. Also emphasized is the need to involve all stakeholders to prevent fear of bias from hindering general acceptance of the tools. This is essential since none of the strategies can be expected to reduce basin-wide agricultural water use by themselves if the overall area of irrigated cultivated land area is not reduced.

The report has been published 2021 in ATB's publication series "Bornimer Agrartechnische Berichte", Volume 104, and can be downloaded free of charge as PDF file: https://www.atb-potsdam.de/fileadmin/generell/BABs/BAB_104_Transformation_Strategies_in_Agriculture.pdf .
